Executive summary

We tested how much of the work that goes into building the Education Endowment Foundation (EEF) Teaching and Learning Toolkit can now be done semi-automatically with large language models (LLMs), without loss of quality relative to manual work. As a test case we chose the strand Metacognition and self-regulation, for which the EEF publishes both the list of source meta-analyses[S1] and the full database of 355 effect sizes from 324 primary studies[S2].

We built a chain of seven steps — from searching for meta-analyses, through their selection, their “unpacking” into primary studies, the eligibility assessment of those studies, to the extraction of statistics and the computation of effect sizes — and at each step compared the output with what the EEF published.

Main findings:

  • Identification and selection of meta-analyses. From a pool of 4,637 records the pipeline selected 36 meta-analyses; these included all 11 meta-analyses listed in the EEF’s technical appendix for the strand[S1] (recall 11/11). The remaining 25 (see the list) are meta-analyses that meet the same criteria but were not used by the EEF. They come from the same publication window — the searches were capped at 2018, the year of the EEF appendix we reproduce — so this is a fuller harvest of the same period, not an extension forward in time.
  • Unpacking meta-analyses into primary studies. The EEF’s own term for this step is “unzipping”: listing the studies included in each meta-analysis and screening them for the database[S3]. From the 36 meta-analyses the model transcribed 1,477 primary studies. Measured against the 224 records the EEF entered into its database in Phase 1:
    • What unpacking recovered. 187 of the 224 records are listed by at least one of the 36 meta-analyses; the model recovered 186 of them (99.5%). The one miss is a study the meta-analysis lists as a 2000 dissertation and the EEF holds as the 2002 journal article: the model transcribed what was listed, and our matcher (author, year ±1, title) did not link the two versions (Section 2, Step 3).
    • What lies outside unpacking. The other 37 records (16.5%) are not included in any of the 36 meta-analyses (7 are merely cited in passing). They come from the second arm of the EEF design — a parallel search for single studies that the Toolkit has run for every strand since 2015 and that the database protocol retains[S4][S5]: 8 journal and conference papers, 10 EEF-funded evaluation reports and 12 dissertations.
    • How reproducible that search is. Only partly, by construction. The EEF publishes the list of databases and, for this strand, three search terms (“Meta-cognition*, executive function, self-regulation*”), but no complete query with limiters or dates; grey literature is found “informally” through Google, Google Scholar and Microsoft Academic; and the EEF deliberately does not use citation searching[S6].
    • What our searches found. Keyword searches of OpenAlex, ERIC, ProQuest, Crossref, Scopus and Semantic Scholar, the OpenAlex citation graph (Step 4) and a scrape of the EEF’s own project pages reach 25 of the 30 as candidates: all 8 papers (7 by keywords, 7 by the citation graph), all 10 EEF reports (6 through ERIC/ProQuest, 8 through the EEF website) and 7 of the 12 dissertations. The 5 not reached are US dissertations from 1992–2005 held only in ProQuest Dissertations & Theses: grey literature that we did not reproduce. “Reached” means present in a candidate pool before screening; it is a statement about coverage, not about precision.
  • Citation-graph expansion (the technique the EEF has used since 2024[S7]) additionally reaches 65% of the studies the EEF added in Phase 2.
  • Eligibility assessment of primary studies. For 338 studies in the EEF database the model assessed the seven EEF criteria: 90% meet all of them, 6% are unclear, and 4% were judged not to meet the criteria — each with a rationale and a page-referenced quotation.
  • Effect-size extraction. We reproduced the EEF formula exactly: Hedges’ g with the small-sample correction (Hedges & Olkin, 1985) and SE as in Wilson’s calculator (Wilson, n.d.). Where the model selected the same outcome as the EEF coder, differences are of the order of 0.001. Differences arise where a study reports many outcomes and one has to be chosen — the bottleneck is the choice, not the arithmetic.
  • Forward update. The same chain applied to the literature of 2022–2026 (34,698 records) yielded 437 eligible studies with computed effect sizes within a few days.
  • Cost. The full identification, selection and unpacking run cost about USD 60 in model fees; effect-size extraction from 316 full texts about USD 74; screening 76,000 records of the post-2021 cohort about USD 44.

The main methodological conclusion: where a task has an unambiguous answer (is this paper a meta-analysis, which studies does it contain, what is the mean in the table), the models reach agreement with the EEF comparable to or higher than agreement between human reviewers. Where a task requires interpretation (is the intervention “metacognitive” in the sense of the EEF definition; which of six outcomes in a paper is “the” outcome), differences between the model and the EEF are not errors on either side but divergent judgements — and they call for an adjudication procedure, not just a recall figure. The report proposes such a procedure.

How this report is organised. Section 1 describes the process we set out to reproduce and why education is a harder test for automation than medicine. Section 2 is the core: step by step, what the pipeline does and how closely its output matches the EEF’s. Section 3 asks what such a comparison can and cannot show, proposes a way of reporting it, and illustrates with concrete records why agreement with the EEF is not the same as correctness. Sections 4–6 cover what the approach could add, its limitations, and what we can offer. The appendices hold the material needed to check or repeat the work. A reader short of time can read the table in Section 2 and Section 3.3.

1 The research problem: semi-automating meta-analyses in education

What this section does. It sets the scene in four steps: how the EEF builds a Toolkit strand (1.1), why that process is worth automating (1.2), what is already known about automating evidence synthesis (1.3), and why education is harder than the medical settings where the strongest results come from (1.4). The point to carry forward is that the EEF process is a chain of discrete, documented steps — which is what makes it reproducible — but several of those steps rest on judgement, and that is where any reproduction, human or automated, will diverge.

1.1 How the EEF Toolkit is built

We begin with the process we are trying to reproduce. The seven steps of our pipeline (Section 2) mirror the EEF’s steps one to one, and the comparison in Section 3 only makes sense against what the EEF actually did — including the parts that were never fully written down.

The EEF Toolkit summarises the evidence on about 30 types of educational intervention (“strands”). Until 2018 each strand’s headline effect was a “meta-meta-analysis”: an average of the pooled effects reported by existing meta-analyses[S8], which the EEF located through database searches, the tables of contents of three review journals and the lists of evidence clearinghouses[S9]. The Evidence Database project (Phase 1, 2018–2021) replaced this with a synthesis at the level of primary studies. For each strand the EEF team (1) took the meta-analyses already underpinning the strand, (2) “unzipped” them — the EEF’s own term — i.e. listed the studies each meta-analysis included and screened them in two stages, title/abstract and full text[S3], (3) assessed each primary study against a common set of criteria (pupils aged 3–18, an intervention classifiable under the strand definition, a normal educational setting, a valid counterfactual comparison, an attainment outcome, an effect size and standard error that can be calculated, plus English-language reporting)[S10], (4) coded each study and extracted its statistics with a team of trained reviewers, 10% of studies double-coded[S11], (5) computed Hedges’ g (Hedges & Olkin, 1985) from post-test means and pooled standard deviations, using Wilson’s online calculator (Wilson, n.d.) for conversions[S12], and pooled the effects in a random-effects model[S13]. Unzipping was never the only route. Since 2015 the Toolkit has run, for every strand, a parallel search for single studies — in bibliographic databases and, informally, for grey literature — so that recent high-quality studies not yet captured by any meta-analysis enter the evidence base[S4]; the database protocol keeps this second arm and lists its sources[S5]. For the metacognition strand this arm contributed the EEF’s own evaluation reports (listed as “single studies” in the strand appendix) and a number of dissertations. Phase 1 was completed in autumn 2021[S14]. Since 2024 (Phase 2) the EEF has been extending each strand with studies found through the OpenAlex citation network, screened with the machine-learning “priority screening” tools of EPPI-Reviewer (Thomas et al., 2023)[S7][S15].

Each of these steps is labour-intensive; the EEF’s plan foresees one Phase-2 update per strand before a “living review” rhythm can be adopted[S14]. As a result the Toolkit is updated rarely and, for this strand, the published evidence base ends in 2021.

1.2 Why automate

There are three reasons. Time: the literature in education grows faster than teams can synthesise it. Reproducibility: if every step is a recorded prompt and a deterministic script, another team can repeat the run and obtain the same result, which cannot be said of manual coding. Reach: automated screening can cover tens of thousands of records, and therefore journals, countries and publication types that a manual team has to exclude from the outset.

1.3 What is already known: a brief literature review

This subsection surveys what is known about LLM-based evidence synthesis. Its purpose is to calibrate expectations: the headline results come from medicine, and the one education-specific study is markedly more cautious. Readers familiar with this literature can move on to 1.4; the key figures are collected in Appendix D.

The automation of evidence synthesis has the longest history in medicine. Cochrane has for years used machine classifiers to recognise randomised trials [the RCT Classifier; Thomas et al. (2021)] and crowd screening [Cochrane Crowd; Thomas et al. (2017)]; tools such as RobotReviewer automate risk-of-bias assessment (Marshall et al., 2016).

Large language models brought a step change. The most prominent study is otto-SR (Cao et al., 2025), a preprint that was also covered in Nature (Pearson, 2025). The authors built a chain of LLM agents for screening and data extraction and reproduced an entire issue of the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (April 2024, 12 reviews, 146,276 citations to screen) in under two days, which they estimate corresponds to about 12 work-years. The model recovered all 64 studies included by the original review authors plus 54 additional eligible studies that had been missed; in three reviews this changed the statistical conclusions. In screening benchmarks otto-SR reached 96.7% sensitivity at 97.9% specificity (dual human screening: 81.7% / 98.1%), and 93.1% accuracy in data extraction (humans: 79.7%). At the same time commentators, among them James Thomas of UCL, the creator of EPPI-Reviewer (Pearson, 2025), pointed out that the results require independent verification and that part of the work — question formulation, search strategy, quality appraisal — remains manual.

Earlier and more cautious studies give a more mixed picture. Tran et al. (2024) showed that GPT-3.5 in title/abstract screening reaches 81–97% sensitivity at only 26–80% specificity, and is therefore suited as a “second reviewer” or pre-filter, not a sole decision-maker. Khraisha et al. (2024), in a pre-registered study covering peer-reviewed and grey literature in several languages, found GPT-4 to perform from poorly to moderately in title/abstract screening but “almost perfectly” in full-text screening with well-constructed prompts. Gartlehner et al. (2024) reported 96% accuracy for Claude 2 in extracting 160 data elements from 10 RCTs. The meta-analysis by Kim et al. (2025) of 14 LLM screening models gives pooled sensitivity and specificity close to 90%.

For education the literature is thinner and less optimistic. Ali et al. (2025) tested machine-learning screening on real systematic reviews in education. Their measure is work saved at 95% recall: the classifier ranks the records from most to least likely to be relevant, a human reads down the list until 95% of the truly relevant studies have been found, and the share of records that never had to be read is the work saved. On this measure the results ranged from 1% (the human had to read practically everything) to 76% (three quarters of the abstracts could be skipped), depending on the review. The methods were those of the pre-LLM era and its first LLMs: classical and deep-learning classifiers trained on each review’s own labels, plus few-shot prompting of GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, which showed the same wide spread — not the current generation of models reading full texts against explicit criteria, as in the studies above and in our pipeline. The lasting finding is the explanation of the spread: performance was predicted by how well relevant and irrelevant studies “separate” in embedding space (R = 0.81). In other words: where the boundaries of the construct are fuzzy, automation works less well — and metacognition is a textbook case of a fuzzy construct.

1.4 Why education is harder than medicine

The literature leaves a question open: do the medical results transfer to education? This subsection gives four reasons to expect that they do not transfer in full. Each of them reappears later as a specific source of disagreement between our pipeline and the EEF — the fuzzy construct in Step 3 and Section 3.1, multi-component interventions in Step 5, outcome reporting in Step 6, and grey literature in the unreached records of Step 3.

Cochrane reviews benefit from four conveniences that education lacks:

  1. Sharp definitions. PICO in medicine rests on unambiguous entities: a drug, a dose, an ICD diagnosis, death. “Metacognition and self-regulation” is a construct whose boundaries are disputed within psychology itself. Is critical-thinking training (Abrami et al., 2008) a metacognitive intervention? Are “thinking skills” (Higgins et al., 2005) the same thing? The EEF answers “yes” to both; our models, applying literally the same definition, answer “no” for part of the studies from these reviews. It is not obvious who is right.
  2. Multi-component interventions. An educational programme usually has several components (learning strategies, group work, feedback). Deciding whether the metacognitive component is “primary”, “secondary” or “incidental” is a judgement, not a fact.
  3. Heterogeneous outcome reporting. Education studies rarely have a single registered primary outcome; a typical paper reports several tests, subscales, subgroups and time points, often with ANCOVA-adjusted rather than raw means. Choosing “the” outcome is a coder’s decision. The EEF does have a written procedure for it: the 2019 protocol states three principles — a good test of the intervention’s impact, an appropriate measure of educational attainment (standardised or national tests preferred over researcher-designed ones), and as direct and fair a measure as possible (single-subject rather than combined scores; wary of “treatment-inherent” tests) — and gives coders a flow diagram[S16], reproduced in Figure 1. The diagram is precise about the form of the estimate: post-test rather than gain score, means and SDs or a standardised mean difference with SE, otherwise a statistic convertible in the Campbell or CMA calculators, with a fixed preference order (post-test adjusted for baseline and clustering, then post-test adjusted for baseline, then post-test only, then gain score)[S17]. But at the one node that matters most for reproducibility — “Can you select the most appropriate from the primary outcome descriptors?” — it relies on the coder’s judgement and, failing that, on “check with review team”. The choice between outcomes is thus principled but not algorithmic, which is exactly why it is hard to reproduce (Section 3).
  4. Grey literature and access. A substantial share of the EEF database consists of dissertations, evaluation reports and articles in regional journals, often not indexed in OpenAlex or ERIC, behind paywalls, or available only as scans.

For these reasons a simple transfer of results from medicine to education would be unwarranted. Hence our test.

2 What we built: the chain of steps and the degree of automation

What this section does. This is the core of the report. For each of the seven steps of the EEF process it states what the EEF does, what our pipeline does instead, how far the step is automated, and how the two outputs compare. The table gives the overview; the comments beneath it expand on the three steps where a single number hides the real picture — unpacking (Step 3), eligibility assessment (Step 5) and effect-size extraction (Step 6). The short version: the steps with an unambiguous answer reproduce the EEF almost exactly; the steps that require judgement do not, and Section 3 argues that they should not be expected to.

Technical details (models, prompts, voting rules, queries) are in Appendix B; full result tables in Appendix C.

1. 2. Screening and selection of meta-analyses Review team; inclusion decided against the strand definition Stage 1: title/abstract, 3 independent Sonnet readings + majority vote, Haiku check; Stage 2: full text for unclear records; Stage 3: deduplication, protocols, versions; Stage 4: Opus verification on full text Full (with optional human adjudication) 36 included, incl. 11/11 EEF; agreement of Stages 1–2 with verification 84%
3. Unpacking (“unzipping”) meta-analyses Manual listing of each meta-analysis’s included studies, then two-stage screening[S3] Model reads the full text (with supplements) and returns the study list coded for metacognitive component, age, year Full 1,477 studies; 83% of the EEF Phase-1 database; 96% of reachable studies
4. Citation-network expansion OpenAlex network-graph searches + EPPI-Reviewer priority screening (Phase 2, since 2024)[S7] One hop over the OpenAlex graph from 505 seed studies, EEF deterministic filter Full 65% of EEF Phase-2 studies; +16 Phase-1 studies

6. The comments that follow expand on the rows where the result is not a single number. Steps 1–2 explain the design choice that runs through the whole pipeline; Step 3 is the longest, because unpacking is where recall is measured and where its limits become visible; Steps 5 and 6 show, respectively, what automation adds that the manual process does not have, and where it hits a bottleneck that is not technical.

Steps 1–2. The most important design decision was to separate assessment from adjudication. At the title/abstract stage the model answers four questions separately (topic, type of paper, outcome, sample), each in three independent readings, and the majority decides; unanimity at the criterion level was 89–95%, which is higher than the typical agreement between two human reviewers in screening (κ 0.5–0.7). Unclear records go to a full-text reading, and everything that passes is verified by a separate, stronger model (Opus), which in 7 of 43 cases did not confirm inclusion — always with a page-referenced quotation on which a human can decide in a minute. The prompt does not mention the EEF or the Toolkit; a comparison with a version that did mention them did not change the decisions for the 11 reference meta-analyses.

Step 3 — what “unpacking” is and how we measured it. A meta-analysis is itself a list of primary studies: typically marked with an asterisk in its reference list, or set out in a table or appendix. “Unpacking” (the EEF’s word is “unzipping”[S3]) means turning that list into database entries — one per study — which are then screened against the Toolkit criteria. In the EEF this was done by hand for each of the strand’s meta-analyses. In our pipeline the model reads the full text of the meta-analysis (plus any supplementary file carrying the list), identifies where the list is, and transcribes each study with first author, year, title and two codes taken from the review’s own description: whether the intervention has a metacognitive/self-regulatory component and whether the sample is of school age.

To measure recall we matched the 1,477 transcribed studies to the EEF database by first author, year (±1) and normalised title. The reference set is the 224 Phase-1 records — the rows the EEF entered in 2018–2021, before the Phase-2 OpenAlex expansion. A record is “reached” if the model listed it from at least one of the 36 meta-analyses. The result is 186 of 224 (83%). The gap of 38 records is, after inspection of every case, 37 records that no meta-analysis includes and 1 genuine miss:

  • 37 records (16.5%) are not included in any of the 36 meta-analyses. Thirty are not mentioned in any of them at all; seven more are mentioned only in passing (an author’s other work, or a namesake, cited in a discussion section — see the next point). The thirty are EEF-funded evaluation reports (10: e.g. Torgerson 2014 Improving Writing Quality, Gorard 2015 Philosophy for Children, Hanley 2015 Thinking, Doing, Talking Science), dissertations and other studies marked “MSR” in the EEF database that come from the EEF’s own single-study searches (12), and a handful of journal and conference papers (8). This is the second arm of the EEF design, not an inconsistency in it: the Toolkit’s parallel single-study search, run for every strand since 2015[S4], carried over into the database protocol[S5], and visible in the strand appendix, which lists the evaluation reports as “single studies” alongside the meta-analyses[S1]. No unpacking procedure, human or automated, can recover these from the meta-analyses; they measure the limit of the unzipping arm, not the quality of the model. In our pipeline the counterpart of that second arm is the citation-graph expansion (Step 4) and the forward search (Step 7).
  • 1 record (0.4%) is a genuine miss; the model recovered 186 of the 187 studies that the meta-analyses actually list. The automatic test initially flagged 8 records as “present in a meta-analysis text but not recovered”, but it is deliberately liberal (surname and year within 120 characters anywhere in the text) and on inspection 7 of the 8 are false alarms: incidental citations of other works by an author of the same surname and year (e.g. Kramarski and Dudai 2009 cited in de Boer et al., 2014, not the Kramarski 2014 study the EEF holds; Tindal and Crawford 2002 in Losinski et al., 2014) and one namesake (the “Liu 2015” in Li et al., 2018 is a different, correlational study). None of these is included in the meta-analysis in question, so none could have been “unpacked” from it. The one real miss is de Koning (2002). Why we did not catch it: Klauer & Phye (2008) include the study under its 2000 dissertation (Inductive reasoning in primary education: Measurement, teaching, transfer, Utrecht) and mention the 2002 journal article only as “see also”; the model transcribed exactly what the meta-analysis lists — the dissertation — whereas the EEF entered the article. Our matcher requires the same first author, a year within ±1 and a matching normalised title; the two versions differ by two years and carry different titles, so the same study under two bibliographic identities was counted as two different studies. This is a limitation of the matching step, not of the reading: the fix is a version-linking rule (same author, overlapping title words, a dissertation and an article within a few years) of the kind the EEF itself applies when it prefers the published version of a study.

How far the second arm can be reproduced. The EEF’s single-study search is documented only in outline: a list of gateways and databases, an example search string for a different strand (Teaching Assistants), and for this strand three search terms — “Meta-cognition*, executive function, self-regulation*”. Grey literature is sought “informally” via Google, Google Scholar and Microsoft Academic, and the protocol states that citation searching and “pearl growing” are deliberately not used[S6]. An exact replication is therefore not possible; what can be tested is whether the 30 records are reachable by systematic, scriptable routes. We used three: keyword searches of primary studies in OpenAlex (title/abstract and full text), ERIC, ProQuest, Crossref, Scopus and Semantic Scholar, run in summer 2026 with the same three-concept vocabulary (intervention × school setting × attainment outcome); the one-hop OpenAlex citation graph of Step 4; and a scrape of the EEF’s project pages. The result, by type of record:

Type of record (n) Keyword searches Citation graph EEF website Any route
Journal and conference papers (8) 7 7 — 8
EEF evaluation reports (10) 6 4 8 10
Dissertations (12) 7 0 1 7
All (30) 20 11 9 25

The one paper the keyword searches miss, Zhang (2019) on working-memory training, uses none of the strand’s vocabulary and is picked up only through citations — a boundary-of-construct case, not a coverage gap. The EEF reports are fully reachable once the EEF’s own website is treated as a source, which is what the EEF itself does. The 5 unreached records are US dissertations from 1992 to 2005 (Burke, Chamberlain, Muoneke, Philbrick, Gudbrandsen) held only in ProQuest Dissertations & Theses and retrievable there by title but not by our subject searches; this is the grey-literature residue we did not reproduce. Two caveats: “reached” means present in a candidate pool, which for the keyword searches is large (tens of thousands of records per database, over half a million for OpenAlex full text), so the cost is in screening rather than in search; and a strict three-concept filter on titles and abstracts passes only 9 of the 30, because reports and dissertations carry sparse abstracts.

Two practical lessons from the gaps that did appear during development: study lists placed in supplementary files outside the PDF are invisible unless attached (fixed by registering the supplements; Smithers et al., 2018; Scruggs et al., 2010), and reviews with 70–120 studies need a long output budget (we raised it to 40,000 tokens). A cross-check with the stronger model (Opus) on the 11 EEF meta-analyses gave an identical set of hits: 137/137.

Step 5. This is the step where semi-automation delivers something the manual process does not: an audit. Assessing 338 studies from the EEF database against the EEF criteria, the model flagged 15 studies that in its judgement do not meet them (e.g. a laboratory study with paid participants; no SDs or t, so the effect cannot be computed with reasonable precision; an academic outcome used only as a baseline variable) and 20 unclear ones. Each of these assessments can be checked in a few minutes, because it comes with a quotation and a page number.

Step 6. We reproduced the EEF arithmetic: the Toolkit uses Hedges’ g with the correction J = 1 − 3/(4N − 9) (Hedges & Olkin, 1985) and the SE as in Wilson’s calculator (Wilson, n.d.); metafor::escalc("SMD") (Viechtbauer, 2010) with default settings gives the same numbers. All remaining discrepancies concern which numbers go into the formula. When the model itself chose the “primary” outcome, the median |Δg| was 0.06, but the distribution has a heavy tail (46% of records differ by more than 0.10) and the pooled estimate was inflated by 0.12. When the model listed all comparisons (median 15 per paper), the EEF figure was among them within 0.10 for 86% of records, and copying errors (SE instead of SD, sign, swapped arms) almost disappeared. The bottleneck is therefore the choice of comparison, not the reading of numbers — more on this in Section 3.

3 The challenge: how to compare an automated result with the EEF’s

What this section does. Sections 1–2 compared our output with the EEF’s mainly through recall. This section steps back and asks what such a comparison can and cannot show. 3.1 explains why recall is insufficient; 3.2 proposes reporting the comparison in four classes that separate errors from judgement calls; 3.3 shows, with concrete records, that the EEF database itself contains both contestable inclusions and notable omissions. The practical consequence is in 3.2: the set of decisions that genuinely needs a human is small and can be listed.

3.1 Recall is simple but insufficient

The standard measure — what share of the EEF studies the pipeline recovered — is easy to compute and we reported it above. It has, however, three weaknesses that became apparent during the work.

First, the EEF database is not a gold standard but one of several possible realisations of the protocol. The pipeline found 25 meta-analyses meeting the EEF criteria that the EEF did not use; from the 11 EEF meta-analyses alone the model extracted 89 metacognitive, school-age, in-window studies that are not in the EEF database (some fail the language or design criterion, but not all); and among the studies the EEF included, the model judged 15 not to meet the criteria. Recall measures agreement with the EEF, not correctness. “More than the EEF” does not automatically mean “better than the EEF”, but “fewer than the EEF” does not automatically mean “worse” either (Section 3.3 shows concrete examples of both directions).

Second, part of the differences are definitional divergences, not errors. The clearest example: from the meta-analysis by Abrami et al. (2008) on critical thinking the EEF entered 8 studies into the database, and from Higgins et al. (2005) on “thinking skills” 16[S2]. Our model, applying the same definition (“the intervention teaches pupils to plan, monitor and evaluate their own learning”), read these studies from the lists but labelled most of them as not metacognitive. If only studies labelled metacognitive are counted, recall drops from 83% to 76% — not because the model failed to find something, but because it drew the boundary of the construct differently. Such a difference has no numerical resolution.

Third, in effect-size extraction there is no single correct answer. A typical paper in the database reports a dozen or more comparisons. When the EEF coder and the model choose the same one, agreement is practically perfect (median |Δg| 0.001). When they choose differently, both choices may be defensible. We checked whether a simple rule (“post-test, full sample, raw means, business-as-usual control”) reproduces the EEF’s choices: it does not. The profile of the EEF’s choices is 59% BAU control but 32% active control; 58% researcher-designed measure, 22% standardised test. No lexicographic rule gave better agreement than the model’s holistic choice, and the model’s holistic choice gives 54% agreement within 0.10. This is consistent with the EEF’s own procedure (Figure 1): its flow diagram fixes the form of the estimate with a strict preference order, but the choice between outcomes rests on three principles and on the coder’s reading of “the most appropriate from the primary outcome descriptors”, with escalation to the review team when the coder is unsure[S16]. Conclusion: the choice of outcome is a coding decision guided by principles rather than by an algorithm, and it cannot be reproduced exactly without such an algorithm — by a human just as much as by a model. Converting the EEF’s three principles into an explicit, testable rule set — and measuring how much of the EEF’s choices it recovers — is a natural joint task.

3.2 From recall to adjudication: a proposed procedure

Where recall ends, qualitative work begins. The purpose of the procedure proposed here is practical: to turn a comparison into a to-do list — to tell a review team which decisions need a human and which do not. We propose that the comparison of the automated result with the EEF (and, in future, of an update with the previous version of the database) be reported in four classes rather than as a single number:

Class Example How to resolve
A. Agreement Study included by both, same effect ±0.05 No action needed
B. Error on one side Study omitted from a meta-analysis list; SE copied as SD; reversed sign Checkable mechanically or in a minute by a human; counted as an error of whichever side made it
C. Definitional divergence Whether critical-thinking training is metacognitive; whether an ANCOVA-adjusted mean counts as a “raw” mean A panel of 2–3 experts, blind to the source of the judgement (human/model), decides on the basis of the quotations presented by both sides; the outcome is recorded as a refinement of the definition for the future
D. Unavailability Study in no available meta-analysis; no full text; scan only Not a measure of pipeline quality; reported separately as the limit of reachability

Under this reporting, the 224 Phase-1 records from Step 3 break down as: 76% class A (recovered and labelled metacognitive), 7% class C (recovered, classified differently), 0.4% class B (one study listed as a dissertation, held by the EEF as the later article — a matching error), 16.5% class D (not included in any meta-analysis), and the model’s “surplus” (89 studies) goes to class C as candidates for panel assessment. This changes the question from “what percentage” to “which decisions require a human” — and that set is small: for the whole strand it is a few dozen definitional rulings and a few dozen outcome choices, not hundreds of hours of coding.

The key property of the models here is that every judgement comes with a rationale and a page-referenced quotation. Adjudication therefore becomes a review of arguments, not a re-reading of papers.

3.3 An illustration: contestable inclusions, and what the database lacks

This subsection is illustrative rather than quantitative. It shows what “the EEF database is not a gold standard” means in practice, in both directions: records that are in the database and arguably should not be, and well-known studies that are not in it. It also shows a by-product of the eligibility assessment (Step 5) that we had not planned for: the model’s free-text notes catch reporting errors that neither peer review nor the EEF’s inclusion screen is designed to catch.

Recall treats every EEF record as correct by definition. Reading the records shows that this assumption deserves a caveat of its own. The EEF criteria screen for design (a comparison group), population, outcome and the availability of an effect size; they do not screen for the internal consistency of the reported numbers or the plausibility of the effect. Under those criteria the model judged four of the five papers below as meeting every criterion — and at the same time, in the free-text note that accompanies each judgement, it flagged the problems shown in the figures. No prompt asked for this; the notes field is simply where the model records what it noticed while reading. All five records belong to the 131 records we attribute to the EEF’s Phase-2 import (Appendix A); the illustrative examples are from India and Nigeria because that is where the most extreme cases happen to be, but the pattern is one of venue and design, not of geography.

Kalaimathi & Julius (2012) — Figure 2; EEF g = 1.12. A three-page paper in the Indian Journal of Applied Research. The design paragraph states that “low score achievers were considered as experimental groups and others control group”: allocation by pretest score, which makes regression to the mean the most parsimonious explanation of any post-test difference. The control group’s pretest mean is not reported. The post-test table gives the experimental group 39.05 and the control group 29.15; the Findings section on the next page then states that the experimental group’s post-test mean is 29.15 — the control value — and takes the gain from a pretest of 16.05 to that number as proof of effectiveness. The model’s note: “Researchers delivered the training themselves. Groups were deliberately non-equivalent (low pretest scorers assigned to treatment), and the control pretest mean is not reported. The reported numbers are internally inconsistent: the Findings give the experimental post-test as 29.15, which is the control mean in the table.” Our pipeline reproduces the EEF’s g to three decimals (1.122). The number is reproducible; the study is not credible.

Sain & Kusum (2021) — Figure 3; EEF g = 0.58. International Journal of Research — Granthaalayah. Table 3 reports means of 89.70 (SD 12.62) and 72.30 (SD 11.28) for two groups of 50 — together with t = 2.95 and p = .19. These values cannot coexist: the means and SDs imply t ≈ 7.3 and a standardised difference of about 1.45, and a t of 2.95 at 98 degrees of freedom cannot have p = .19. The EEF coder used the t statistic and obtained 0.58; the model’s means route gives 1.44. The model’s note: “reported statistics are internally inconsistent (t=2.95, p=.19 vs. means/SDs implying a much larger t; df=99 with N=100); the procedure section is empty.” Here the choice of computation route changes the effect size by a factor of 2.5, and nothing in the paper tells us which of the two numbers the authors got right.

Alhassan (2017) — Figure 4; EEF g = 3.32, the second-largest effect in the strand. Journal of Education and Practice, a journal that describes itself as peer-reviewed. The three results tables, reproduced together in the figure, do not survive being read side by side. Table 1 (pretest) gives both groups N = 31; Tables 2 and 3 (post-tests) give the experimental group N = 333. In Table 2, the knowledge post-test, the experimental mean is 3.03 with SD 0.996 — the control group scores 6.23, i.e. twice as high — while the text under the table announces a significant difference “in favor of the experimental group”. The value 3.03 is the experimental group’s pretest mean from Table 1: a pretest figure was pasted into a post-test table, and with it the direction of the effect flipped on paper. Taken literally, Table 2 says the intervention cut knowledge scores by about three standard deviations; our pipeline’s reading of that table indeed yields g = −2.87. In Table 3, with N = 33 and 31, the means and SDs imply t ≈ 13.4, not the printed 8.84. The model’s note: “The author designed the materials and ran the evaluation. There is one class per arm, analysed at pupil level with t-tests. The tables contain inconsistencies: the knowledge-test means appear swapped relative to the text, the experimental n is printed as 333 and is 31 at pretest, and the reported t values do not match the means and SDs.” None of this requires expertise to notice — an N ten times the sample, a post-test mean identical to the pretest mean, a table contradicting its own caption text — which is the point: the paper passed a peer review that evidently did not read the tables, and then passed the EEF’s inclusion screen, which does not look for this either.

Nbina & Viko (2010) — Figure 5; EEF g = 5.80, the largest effect in the database. The EEF lists the paper in Academic Leadership: The Online Journal (2010); the full text we obtained is the same paper reprinted in the Journal of Research in Education and Society (2012). The participants’ “average age is 0.4 years”; a chemistry self-assessment intervention is described as instruction in “solving mathematical problems”; the control N is 95 in one table and 97 in another; and the ANCOVA F for the treatment effect is 1,621.9, which corresponds to a difference of almost six standard deviations between two groups of about 96 pupils drawn from four schools (one intact class each) and analysed at pupil level. The model’s note: “The researcher developed the SAIP and delivered it himself; only 4 schools were allocated (one class each) but the ANCOVA is at pupil level with no clustering adjustment; there are internal inconsistencies (control N 97 vs 95, ‘MAT’ labels, mathematical problems, implausible mean age, and an implausibly large F).”

Karahroudi & Reddy (2014) — Figure 6; EEF g = 3.14. The IOSR Journal of Engineering, for a study of writing errors among fifth-graders in Hyderabad. Two consecutive tables carry the same number; the text reports t = 6.98 as “greater than the table value .000” and concludes that there is no significant difference; the design is described as both “randomly assigned” and “quasi-experimental”. This is the one record of the five the model did not pass: it rated the setting criterion unclear because the text never says the training took place in school, and noted the contradictions in the design description.

What the examples have in common, and how much they weigh. All five share a profile: a small journal outside the major citation indexes; one intact class per arm; the researcher as developer, deliverer and assessor; a researcher-made test; pupil-level analysis with no adjustment for clustering; and an effect size that would be remarkable in any field. The profile is not confined to these five. Nineteen of the 355 records in the strand have g ≥ 2; thirteen of them are Phase-2 records, and fifteen pass every EEF criterion in the model’s assessment. Across the whole strand the model’s notes flag some internal inconsistency in the reported numbers in 52 records (15%) — from the trivial (a lesson length given as both 30 and 45 minutes) to the kind that changes the effect size. The flagged records have a pooled effect of 1.05 against 0.42 for the rest. Stratified by the EEF’s own data, the 89 records from outside Western high-income countries pool to 1.11 (median 0.96) against 0.51 (median 0.43) for the 253 Western records, and the 46 randomised trials to 0.41. Because every included record contributes to the strand’s headline estimate, these are not cosmetic problems: a simple random-effects pool of all 355 records gives 0.47, and 0.42 once the 19 records with g ≥ 2 are removed.

None of this requires a new method. What the model adds is that the problems are detected at reading time, for every record, in a structured field, and at no extra cost; they are the raw material for a reporting-consistency flag that could route a record to human checking or to a sensitivity analysis before it enters a pooled estimate. In the terms of Section 3.2 these are class-B events — checkable in a minute by a human once pointed out — that the EEF’s current procedure has no step to catch.

The mirror image: what the EEF lacks and the pipeline has. Unpacking the 36 pipeline meta-analyses produced 422 unique studies that the model labelled metacognitive and school-age and that are not in the EEF strand. These have not yet been through Steps 5 and 6 (the eligibility assessment and extraction were run on the EEF records only), so they are candidates, not confirmed inclusions. Ranked by citation count, however, the top of the list contains studies that are canonical in the field:

Study Citations (OpenAlex) Where the pipeline found it EEF status
Brown et al. (1996) — transactional strategies instruction, grade 2. Journal of Educational Psychology 349 Dignath et al. (2008), Table 17 — one of the EEF’s own eleven meta-analyses Not in any strand
Englert et al. (1991) — cognitive strategy instruction in writing with self-talk. American Educational Research Journal 388 Graham et al. (2012); Marzano (1998) Not in any strand
Sawyer et al. (1992) — SRSD with explicit self-regulation. Journal of Educational Psychology 258 Graham et al. (2012) Not in any strand (the strand holds more than a dozen later SRSD studies)
Yarrow & Topping (2001) — metacognitive prompting in collaborative writing. British Journal of Educational Psychology 235 Graham et al. (2012) Not in any strand
Adey & Shayer (1993) — cognitive acceleration (CASE), far transfer. Cognition and Instruction 188 Dignath & Büttner (2008) Not in any strand (Adey 1990 and 2002 are in)
Klingner & Vaughn (1996) — reciprocal teaching, LD pupils. Elementary School Journal 312 Swanson (2001) In Collaborative learning, not here
Jitendra et al. (2000) — summarisation strategy and self-monitoring. Journal of Special Education 192 de Boer et al. (2018); Scruggs et al. (2010) In Reading comprehension strategies (g = 1.78), not here
Stevens et al. (1991) — direct instruction in comprehension strategies. Journal of Educational Psychology 184 Fauzan (2003) — one of the EEF’s own eleven In Collaborative learning, not here
Van Keer & Vanderlinde (2010) — cross-age peer tutoring in reading strategies. Middle Grades Research Journal — Donker et al. (2014); de Boer et al. (2014) and one further meta-analysis In Peer tutoring and Reading comprehension, not here

Two things about this list deserve attention. First, two of the studies sit in the reference lists of meta-analyses the EEF itself unpacked for this strand, and the strand already cross-lists 49 of its records with other strands, so the absences are boundary decisions or oversights rather than unawareness. Second, the comparison with the previous paragraph is stark: a database that contains Nbina & Viko (2010) with g = 5.80 and Alhassan (2017) with g = 3.32 does not contain Brown et al. (1996) or Sawyer et al. (1992). We do not claim that the nine studies above would all survive the eligibility assessment, nor that their inclusion would change the headline estimate much — most of them report moderate effects. The point is narrower: an automated pass over the same sources surfaces both kinds of discrepancy, in a form that a human can adjudicate in minutes, and the EEF’s database has not had that pass.

4 Potential for extension

What this section does. Having established how well the pipeline reproduces the existing database, we turn to what it could add. Three directions: backward — a fuller database for existing strands under the same criteria (4.1); forward — a living synthesis that keeps the database current (4.2); and broader — coverage beyond the journals and languages a manual team can afford (4.3). Each is stated with the numbers we already have, not as a promise.

4.1 Backward: a fuller database for existing strands

Three observations show that the EEF database for this strand could be larger under the same criteria:

  • Meta-analyses not used by the EEF. 25 of the 36 included meta-analyses do not appear in the EEF appendix; they contributed 49 studies that the EEF has in its database (so the EEF reached them another way), but also hundreds of studies the EEF does not have.
  • Studies in the EEF meta-analyses that the EEF did not enter. 89 metacognitive, school-age studies from the 11 EEF meta-analyses alone. Some (47 from Klauer & Phye, 2008, almost all German-language; 14 from Losinski et al., 2014, single-case designs) fail the EEF criteria; the remaining ~28 are candidates for full screening.
  • Citation network. One hop over the OpenAlex graph from 505 seed studies yields 35,239 candidates after the deterministic filter; at a threshold of “≥ 2 links to seeds” 8,792 remain, among them 63 EEF studies unreachable from meta-analyses. The same hop yields candidates the EEF does not have — screening them is a matter of days, not months.

The same chain can be run for the other Toolkit strands without changing the code — only the strand definition in the prompt and the search vocabulary change.

4.2 Forward: living synthesis

The forward direction is where the case for automation is strongest, because the EEF’s own plan — one Phase-2 update per strand — is limited by labour, not by method. We tested it directly.

We ran the chain on the literature of 2022–2026: 34,698 records after searching, 3,057 after title/abstract screening, 855 with a full text obtained, 437 eligible under the EEF criteria, 339 with a computable g. The analysis showed that the new cohort is dominated by quasi-experimental studies from outside Western countries (269 of 305), with larger effects; after stratification by country and design the effects converge with the EEF’s (Western countries: EEF 0.51 vs 0.57; RCTs: 0.41 vs 0.53). This result alone — that the composition of the post-2021 literature is different and that the comparison requires stratification — is a finding that could not have been obtained in reasonable time without automation.

The EEF’s own protocols already name “living reviews” as the end state of the database project[S18][S15]. The operating model of a “living Toolkit” would look as follows: quarterly automated search, screening and extraction of new records; a list of class-C rulings for the panel; an update of the pooled estimate with versioning. The computational cost of one cycle for one strand is tens, not thousands, of dollars.

4.3 Broader coverage

Automated screening need not be restricted to English-language journals indexed in the main databases. The models read full texts in many languages (although the EEF criterion restricts the database to English), handle reports and dissertations, and the cost of screening is linear in the number of records. This opens the possibility of deliberately widening (or deliberately not widening) the Toolkit’s scope, with full documentation of what was included and why.

5 Limitations

What this section does. Every result above should be read with the following limitations in mind. They are listed roughly in order of how much they could change the conclusions.

  • One strand. The results concern metacognition and self-regulation — a strand with fuzzy construct boundaries. For strands with sharper definitions (e.g. reducing class size) we expect better agreement; for even fuzzier ones (e.g. social and emotional learning) worse. This needs testing.
  • Access to full texts remains a manual bottleneck: 8 of the 355 EEF studies have no available full text, 7 are scans without a text layer, 11 are dissertations with restricted access. In the post-2021 cohort a full text was obtained for 855 of 3,057 records that passed screening.
  • Models change. The results refer to specific model versions (Claude Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, Opus 5.5); the pipeline records model identifiers, prompts and token counts, so the run is reproducible, but newer models may give different results.
  • No human panel yet. The adjudication procedure of Section 3.2 is a proposal; we have not yet run a blinded panel on class-C cases. This is the natural next step, ideally in collaboration with the EEF team.
  • Outcome selection in extraction requires either a written EEF rule or a second model pass that only selects among the listed comparisons. Both variants are feasible; neither is yet validated.

6 What we can offer

What this section does. The preceding sections lead to four concrete things IBE PIB can offer the EEF, or any comparable evidence team, in the order in which they could be started.

  1. Reproduction of any Toolkit strand under the procedure described, with a report in the four agreement classes and a list of rulings for an EEF panel.
  2. An audit of the existing database — an assessment of every study against the EEF criteria with quotations, as in Step 5.
  3. A forward update — the 2022–2026 cohort for selected strands, stratified by country and design.
  4. Joint validation of the adjudication procedure — a blinded panel of EEF and IBE PIB experts on class-C cases, whose outcome would at the same time refine the strand definitions.

Appendices

What the appendices contain. The material a reader needs to check or reproduce the claims in the main text: how we reconstructed the EEF’s reference set (A), how each step of the pipeline is built (B), the full result tables (C), key figures from the literature (D) and where the files are (E). They are written for a technical reader and assume the main text has been read.

Appendix A. The EEF reference set and its reconstruction

This appendix documents exactly what the pipeline was compared against, and the one inference on which several numbers in the main text depend — the split of the EEF database into Phase 1 and Phase 2.

Sources. The technical appendix of the strand Metacognition and self-regulation (2018 edition of the Toolkit strand page) states that the evidence rests on eleven meta-analyses and lists them with their pooled effects (Abrami et al., 2008; Chiu, 1998; de Boer et al., 2014; Dignath et al., 2008; Donker et al., 2014; Fauzan, 2003; Haller et al., 1988; Higgins et al., 2005; Klauer & Phye, 2008; Losinski et al., 2014; Zheng, 2016)[S1]. An earlier version of the appendix lists seven of them and additionally references the single-case review by Perry et al. (2012) and the narrative review by Jacob & Parkinson (2015); we track these two but do not count them. The effect-size database (355 records) was retrieved from the study-level table of the strand’s current technical-appendix page[S2]; each record carries author, year, title, g, SE, confidence interval, country, design and (for part of the records) a DOI or an OpenAlex URL.

Phase 1 vs Phase 2. The EEF describes Phase 1 (unzipping of the strand’s meta-analyses plus single-study searches, completed autumn 2021) and Phase 2 (OpenAlex-based backfilling from 2024) as separate stages[S14][S7], but the public table does not label rows by phase. We infer the split from the identifier structure: identifiers below 90,000,000 (224 records, 201 studies) carry the 2018–2021 entries, identifiers ≥ 90,000,000 (131 records, 123 studies) were imported in one alphabetical batch and contain no study reachable from the strand’s meta-analyses, which is what a Phase-2 import should look like. This is our inference, not an EEF statement.

What in Phase 1 does not come from meta-analyses. 30 Phase-1 records appear in none of the 36 meta-analyses: EEF evaluation reports (e.g. Torgerson 2014 Improving Writing Quality, Torgerson 2018 IPEELL, Gorard 2015 Philosophy for Children, Hanley 2015, Dorsett 2014) — which the strand appendix lists as “single studies” next to the meta-analyses[S1] — and dissertations and papers marked “MSR” in the database, which come from the EEF’s own single-study searches provided for in the protocol[S5] (including 7 US dissertations with no OpenAlex record).

Identifier coverage. 338/355 EEF records could be matched to an OpenAlex record (DOI 171, EEF URL 114, title 53); 17 have no OpenAlex record.

Appendix B. Pipeline architecture

This appendix gives, for each of the seven steps, the models, prompts, decision rules and volumes needed to repeat the run, followed by the costs. The numbering follows the steps of Section 2.

B.1 Step 1 — identification of meta-analyses (four routes)

Route Source Query (abridged) Records Recall of 11 EEF MAs
A_openalex OpenAlex title+abstract: (metacognit* OR self-regulat* OR executive function* OR learning strateg*) AND (meta-analy* OR quantitative synthesis OR systematic review), to 2018 2,377 9/11
A_eric ERIC the same in the title/description fields 146 7/11
B tables of contents of Review of Educational Research (from 2000), Educational Research Review, Review of Education all articles 1,798 5/11
C Campbell (ISSN), EPPI-Centre, Best Evidence Encyclopedia, WWC (not accessible to scripts) all items 697 1/11
Total after deduplication 4,767 (4,637 after removing non-English records) 11/11

Two EEF meta-analyses (Higgins et al., 2005; Klauer & Phye, 2008) carry no strand term in the title or abstract and are reachable only via routes B or C; this justifies keeping the keyword-free routes.

B.2 Step 2 — selection (Stages 1–4)

Stage 1 (title/abstract). Four criteria assessed separately: TOPIC (an intervention with a metacognitive/self-regulatory component), TYPE (a meta-analysis or quantitative synthesis of intervention studies), OUTCOME (school attainment), SAMPLE (school-age pupils). Primary model: Claude Sonnet 5.5, three independent readings, majority decision per criterion; check model: Claude Haiku 5.5, one reading. Overall decision: include if all criteria include; exclude if any criterion exclude; otherwise unclear. Records without an abstract: if the title unambiguously excludes, the model quotes the title and excludes; otherwise unclear. Route B (journals) has a two-step path: first TYPE (is it a meta-analysis), then the rest on the full text.

Agreement (keyword path, 2,374 records): unanimity of the three readings — TOPIC 95%, TYPE 92%, OUTCOME 89%, SAMPLE 92%; agreement of the Sonnet majority with Haiku on the overall decision 91%, with not a single include/exclude pair. For comparison, agreement between two human reviewers in title/abstract screening reported in the literature is usually in the range κ 0.5–0.7.

Stage 2 (full text). 502 records unclear after Stage 1; one Sonnet 5.5 reading on the full text (OpenAlex OA, ERIC, downloaded PDFs; manually supplied files treated identically). If still unclear after the full text — two additional readings and a vote as in Stage 1.

Stage 3 (consolidation). 49 included → 43: 1 duplicate, 2 protocols, 1 superseded version (preprint vs publication) and 2 papers with a non-English full text (Kim 2016, Kim 2018 — English abstracts, Korean texts) were removed.

Stage 4 (verification). Claude Opus 5.5, one reading of the full text (41) or title/abstract (2 with no available text). Result: 36 include, 2 unclear, 5 exclude; 11/11 EEF meta-analyses confirmed. Exclusions mostly concerned TOPIC (correlational reviews, neurological rehabilitation), each with a quotation.

Prompt. Neutral: it mentions neither the EEF, the Toolkit nor any reference list. A comparison with an earlier version that did mention the EEF, on a 100-record pilot, did not change the decisions for the reference meta-analyses.

B.3 Step 3 — unpacking

Claude Sonnet 5.5, one reading of the meta-analysis full text (up to 800,000 characters, up to 40,000 output tokens — necessary for reviews with 100+ studies, e.g. Abrami et al., 2008; Graham et al., 2012). Supplements are appended to the text (e.g. Supplementary Table 2 of Smithers et al., 2018, or the publisher’s reference list for Scruggs et al., 2010). The model indicates the source of the list (asterisks in the bibliography, a table, an appendix) and returns for each study: first author, year, title, metacognitive component (yes/no/unclear) and sample age (school-age/not/unclear) according to the review’s own coding, plus a note on discrepancies (e.g. declared vs listed number of studies).

Matching to the EEF database: normalised (first author, year ±1, title); a hit on one record counts for all records of the same study (multiple effect sizes). Cross-check: the same prompt with Opus 5.5 on the 11 EEF meta-analyses — identical set of hits (137/137), cost USD 4.52.

B.4 Step 4 — graph expansion

Seeds: 505 unique studies from Step 3 (metacognitive, school-age, 1990–2021); 359 with an OpenAlex record. One hop: bibliographies (referenced_works), citing works (cites:), related works (related_works). 50,975 candidates → 35,239 after the EEF deterministic filter (year 1990–2021, English or unknown language, not a paratext, not an included meta-analysis).

B.5 Step 5 — eligibility assessment of primary studies

Claude Opus 5.5, one reading of the full text. Seven EEF criteria: POPULATION, INTERVENTION, SETTING, DESIGN, OUTCOME, EFFECT_SIZE, LANGUAGE; each rated meets/unclear/fails, with a quotation and page number; additionally the role of the metacognitive component (primary/secondary/incidental/none) and a quality note (clustering, attrition, author = developer of the intervention). Full texts: 340 OK, 7 scans, 8 missing; dissertations (11) excluded from the tables.

B.6 Step 6 — extraction and computation of effect sizes

Two prompt variants. v1: the model selects one primary attainment outcome and copies the statistics. v3: the model lists every comparison (groups, measure, time point, subgroup, type of means: raw/adjusted, statistics) without choosing; selection and computation follow in code. For 316 documents v3 produced 6,513 comparisons (median ~15 per paper), 5,185 computable.

Computation (deterministic, Python/R):

  • d = (M_t − M_c) / s_pooled, where s_pooled = √[((n_t − 1)SD_t² + (n_c − 1)SD_c²) / (n_t + n_c − 2)]
  • g = J · d, J = 1 − 3/(4(n_t + n_c) − 9)
  • Var(g) = (n_t + n_c)/(n_t · n_c) + g²/(2(n_t + n_c)); SE = √Var
  • alternative routes: from t (d = t·√(1/n_t + 1/n_c)), from F(1, df) (d = √F·√(1/n_t + 1/n_c)), reported d
  • pooled model: random effects, REML [metafor::rma; Viechtbauer (2010)]; the Paule–Mandel estimator (Paule & Mandel, 1982) gives practically the same results (0.798 vs 0.801 for 128 studies).

Verification of the EEF formula on 145 pairs with the same outcome: median ES_EEF / d (without J) = 0.990 = median J; median ES_EEF / g = 1.000; 107 vs 38 pairs closer to g than to d (p < 0.0001). SE_EEF / SE_Wilson: median 1.002, 81% within ±10%. The Toolkit applies no blanket clustering correction.

B.7 Step 7 — the 2022–2026 cohort

OpenAlex search analogous to route A but for primary studies (not meta-analyses), years 2022–2026: 34,698 records → title/abstract screening (earlier pipeline version, Claude Haiku 4.5) → 3,057 → full texts 855 → EEF criteria assessment + extraction in one pass → 437 eligible → 339 with a computable g → 305 with a sign.

Pooled models (REML): EEF, 355 records — 0.680 [0.609; 0.751], τ² 0.41; v1 on 319 — 0.819 [0.718; 0.921], τ² 0.79; v3 rule A on 280 — 0.756 [0.665; 0.847], τ² 0.54; v3 oracle on 295 — 0.716 [0.635; 0.797], τ² 0.45.

Sources of v1 discrepancies (most frequent first): sign convention (20 records; “lower is better” scales, swapped arms); ANCOVA SEs copied as SDs (s_pooled underestimated, g of 5–6 instead of 0.2–2.5); contrast choice (e.g. Fuchs 2003: transfer+SRL vs transfer 0.03 against the EEF’s vs control 2.8); EEF values not reproducible from the paper’s tables (Teong 2003, Zohar 1994, Collins 1991); unlabelled test statistics.

Profile of the comparisons chosen by the EEF (204 records matched to v3): post-test 96%, full sample 94%, measure in the intervention domain 90%, raw means 87%, BAU control 59% / active 32%, researcher-designed measure 58% / standardised 22%.

Appendix D. Literature review — key figures

Numerical details of the studies discussed in Section 1.3, for readers who want the figures rather than the narrative.

  • Cao et al. (2025) (otto-SR): reproduction of the April 2024 issue of the Cochrane Database (12 reviews, 146,276 citations, < 48 h); screening: sensitivity 96.7% / specificity 97.9% vs 81.7% / 98.1% for dual human screening; extraction: 93.1% vs 79.7%; 64/64 original studies recovered, 54 additional, conclusions changed in 3 reviews. Coverage and critical voices: Pearson (2025).
  • Tran et al. (2024): 5 reviews, 22,665 citations; balanced rule: sensitivity 81–97%, specificity 26–80%; sensitive rule: sensitivity 95–100%, specificity 2–47%.
  • Khraisha et al. (2024): pre-registered; GPT-4; peer-reviewed and grey literature, several languages; title/abstract screening: none to moderate agreement after correction for chance; full text with reliable prompts: “almost perfect”.
  • Gartlehner et al. (2024): Claude 2, 10 RCTs, 160 elements, accuracy 96.3%, test–retest 95–97%.
  • Kim et al. (2025): 14 LLM screening models; SROC: sensitivity and specificity about 90%.
  • Ali et al. (2025): real systematic reviews in education; classical and deep-learning classifiers plus few-shot GPT-3.5 and GPT-4; work saved at 95% recall from 1.2% to 75.6%, with a similarly wide spread for the LLMs; cluster separability in embedding space predicts effectiveness (R = 0.81).
  • Cochrane tools: the RCT Classifier (Thomas et al., 2021), Cochrane Crowd and Screen4Me (Thomas et al., 2017); RobotReviewer for risk-of-bias assessment (Marshall et al., 2016); EPPI-Reviewer (Thomas et al., 2023) with priority screening and OpenAlex integration — the tool used by the EEF in Phase 2.

Appendix E. Files and reproducibility

S1 Strand appendix (2018 ed.)

Education Endowment Foundation. Teaching and Learning Toolkit: Metacognition and self-regulation — Technical Appendix (2018 edition of the strand page, in force until the 2021 redesign).

Location in the document: 'Evidence Rating' and 'Summary of effects' table

Overall, the evidence is rated as extensive. There are eleven meta-analyses with seven undertaken in the last 10 years. […] The majority of the pooled effects from the meta-analyses fall in the range 0.44 to 0.71. — Summary of effects, Meta-analyses: Abrami et al. (2008) 0.34; Chiu (1998) 0.67; de Boer, Donker & van der Werf (2014) 0.57; Dignath, Buettner & Langfeldt (2008) 0.62; Donker et al. (2014) 0.66; Fauzan (2003) 0.50; Haller, Child & Walberg (1988) 0.71; Higgins, Hall, Baumfield & Moseley (2005) 0.62; Klauer & Phye (2008) 0.69; Losinski et al. (2014) 0.90; Zheng (2016) 0.44. Single studies: Crawford & Skipp (2014); Dorsett et al. (2014); Gorard et al. (2015); Hanley et al. (2016); Hanley, Slavin & Elliott (2015); Motteram et al. (2016); NIESR (2015); Torgerson et al. (2014); Tracy, Reid & Graham (2009).

Note. An earlier version of the same appendix (Wayback snapshot of 19 July 2021 of the PDF, local file EEF_Technical_Appendix_Metacognition_wb20210719.pdf) lists seven meta-analyses (without de Boer 2014, Fauzan 2003, Losinski 2014 and Zheng 2016) and the tracked reviews Perry et al. (2012) and Jacob & Parkinson (2015). We use the eleven-item list; Perry (2012) and Jacob & Parkinson (2015) are tracked but not counted.

S2 EEF database (strand page)

Education Endowment Foundation. Metacognition and self-regulation — Technical Appendix (current Toolkit page), interactive study-level evidence table and forest plot (one row per effect size: study, year, country, design, effect size, standard error, confidence interval, weight, DOI / link).

Location in the document: study-level table of the strand, retrieved programmatically in 2026 (355 rows; 29 publications contribute more than one row)

Per row the page publishes: effect size (standardised mean difference), standard error, 95% confidence interval, weight, and bibliographic fields incl. abstract, DOI and document links. Our check: the confidence interval equals effect size ± 1.96 × SE for 355 of 355 rows.

Note. The split of the 355 rows into Phase 1 (224 rows, database identifiers below 90 000 000) and Phase 2 (131 rows, identifiers ≥ 90 000 000, imported in alphabetical order) is our inference from the identifier structure, not an EEF statement.

EEF Toolkit — technical appendix page

S3 EEF protocol 2019

Higgins, S., Villanueva Aguilera, A. B., Dobson, E., Gascoine, L., Katsipataki, M., & Rajab, T. (2019). EEF Evidence Database: Protocol and Analysis Plan, version 1.1, June 2019. Durham University / Education Endowment Foundation.

Location in the document: p. 4, 'Criteria for inclusion and exclusion of studies in the review'; flow chart in Appendix A, p. 17

The initial set of studies for this review will be identified from the current version of the EEF-Sutton Trust Teaching and Learning Toolkit. Nearly all of the strands are based on meta-analyses and systematic reviews which have been identified through a systematic updating process (EEF, 2018) since the initial version of the Toolkit was published by the Sutton Trust in 2011 (Higgins et al. 2011). These meta-analyses will be systematically 'unzipped' so that the included studies which contribute to the overall pooled effect are identified and screened (a two-stage process of title and abstract and then full text screening) for inclusion in the database. A flow chart describing this process can be found in Appendix A.

S4 Toolkit manual 2018

Education Endowment Foundation (2018). Teaching and Learning Toolkit: Technical appendix and process manual (v.01, July 2018).

Location in the document: section 6, 'Single studies', and section 9, 'Single studies'

Since 2015, single studies retrieved from a parallel search have also been used where available to create a new but basic meta-analysis for all strands which is then included in the meta-meta-analysis calculation. This is to ensure that recent high quality single studies which have not yet been included in any meta-analyses are reflected in the overall effect size estimate. […] in order to ensure that recent high quality studies not yet included in reviews are captured by the search process, a separate search of single studies is done for each Toolkit strand.

Note. The 2019 database protocol carries this arm over: the single-study search 'update[s] the existing single studies identified for the Toolkit' and includes 'informal searching for grey literature (reports and unpublished studies)'. The strand appendix accordingly lists nine 'single studies' (EEF evaluation reports) next to the eleven meta-analyses.

S5 EEF protocol 2019

Higgins, S. et al. (2019). EEF Evidence Database: Protocol and Analysis Plan, version 1.1, June 2019.

Location in the document: pp. 6–7, 'Search strategy for identification of relevant single studies'

Where there are no existing meta-analyses or systematic reviews with quantitative data in the existing Toolkit strands, a new systematic search will be undertaken for primary studies to update the existing single studies identified for the Toolkit. These sources will be used (gateways and databases): First search (Article First, ECO, Papers First, World Cat Dissertations), EBSCO (BEI, Education Abstracts, Education Administration Abstracts, ERIC, PsycArticles, PsycINFO), Taylor and Francis (Educational Research Abstracts Online), ProQuest (ProQuest Dissertations and theses (Global)), Elsevier (Science Direct), Thomson Reuters (Web of Science). In addition, informal searching for 'grey' literature (reports and unpublished studies) is undertaken using Google, Google Scholar and Microsoft Academic.

S7 EEF Phase 2 protocol 2024

Higgins, S., Villanueva Aguilera, B., Dobson, E., Gascoine, L., Kalambouka, A., Katsipataki, M., Reardon, J., Rovida, M., & Uwimpuhwe, G. (2024). EEF Evidence Database Phase 2: Protocol and Analysis Plan, January 2024. Education Endowment Foundation.

Location in the document: 'Background and review rationale' and 'Search strategy for identification of studies'

A limitation of the current version of the database is that the coverage of studies in each strand varies according to the inclusion criteria of the underpinning reviews which were used to identify the screened studies. […] The aim of this phase of the database project, therefore, is to update each of the strands by systematically searching for missing studies using OpenAlex, an open source bibliographic database, and some of the machine learning tools for search and screening available within EPPI-Reviewer. […] Studies for each strand will be identified using keywords and terms developed in Phase 1 […], together with the studies screened previously for each of the Toolkit strands. These studies will then be used to identify potentially similar studies via network graph searches in OpenAlex, a database of millions of interconnected research references or 'entities', using the machine learning tools in EPPI-Reviewer 6.

S8 Toolkit manual 2018

Education Endowment Foundation (2018). Sutton Trust–EEF Teaching and Learning Toolkit & EEF Early Years Toolkit: Technical appendix and process manual (working document v.01, July 2018).

Location in the document: section 1, description of the strand summary

An estimate of the average impact of relevant interventions, presented in terms of expected months' progress. This is based on an effect size estimate derived from a synthesis of meta-analytical effect sizes in existing meta-analyses and quantitative systematic reviews, where there is sufficient data to combine these estimates. This calculation is referred to as a 'meta-meta-analysis'. The effect size estimate itself is included in the technical appendix to each strand.

S9 Toolkit manual 2018

Education Endowment Foundation (2018). Teaching and Learning Toolkit: Technical appendix and process manual (v.01, July 2018).

Location in the document: sections 5.1–5.3, 'Identification'

Searches are undertaken for systematic reviews with quantitative data (where effect sizes are reported but not pooled) and meta-analyses (where effect sizes are combined to provide a pooled estimated of effect) of intervention research in education in each of the areas of the Toolkit. […] When searching for new meta-analyses and systematic reviews these terms are also included: 'meta-analysis'; 'quantitative synthesis'; 'systematic review'. […] The search engines and gateways used are: FirstSearch, EBSCO, JSTOR, Web of Science, Science Direct, Google Scholar and ProQuest Dissertations. The following review journals are also screened for recent systematic reviews and meta-analyses: […] Review of Educational Research, […] Education Research Review and […] Review of Education […]. Other resources that are checked are the pages of What Works Clearing House (WWC), Best Evidence Encyclopaedia (BEE) and the Evidence for Policy and Practice Information (EPPI) Centre, […] The Campbell Collaboration and The Cochrane Database.

S10 EEF protocol 2019

Higgins, S. et al. (2019). EEF Evidence Database: Protocol and Analysis Plan, version 1.1, June 2019.

Location in the document: pp. 5–6, inclusion and exclusion criteria table

Inclusion criteria: The majority of the sample (>50%) on which the analysis is based are learners or pupils aged between 3-18 […]. Evaluates the impact of an educational intervention or approach, including named or clearly defined programmes and recognisable approaches classifiable according to the Toolkit strand definitions (see Appendix B). The intervention or approach is undertaken in a normal educational setting or environment for the learners involved […]. A valid counterfactual comparison between those receiving the educational intervention or approach and those not receiving it. Assessment of educational or cognitive achievement which reports quantitative results from testing of attainment or learning outcomes […]. A quantitative estimate of the impact […] can be calculated or estimated in the form of an effect size (standardised mean difference) with its standard error based on a counterfactual comparison.

S11 EEF protocol 2019

Higgins, S. et al. (2019). EEF Evidence Database: Protocol and Analysis Plan, version 1.1, June 2019.

Location in the document: p. 9, 'Details of study coding categories'

All coding activities (i.e., abstract screening, full-text review, study features coding, as well as effect size extraction) will be carried out by a team of reviewers, each working independently but discussing and resolving queries, when necessary eliciting a third opinion from the core project team. All coders receive training and have to achieve an agreed level of reliability to be included in the coding team. A 10% sample of studies (per coder and per strand) are double coded to assess reliability rates.

S12 EEF protocol 2019

Higgins, S. et al. (2019). EEF Evidence Database: Protocol and Analysis Plan, version 1.1, June 2019.

Location in the document: pp. 9–10, 'Statistical procedures and conventions'; footnote 7, p. 6

The key metric used is the Standardised Mean Difference (d-index) or effect size. […] For studies that report descriptive statistics for continuous measures of pupil attainment outcomes, the post-intervention mean of the control group will be subtracted from the post-intervention mean of the intervention group and the resulting difference will be divided by the pooled standard deviation, adjusted for sample size (Hedges' g). An accompanying standard error (representing the 95% confidence interval) will also be recorded. […] [footnote 7] Such as by using the conversions available in programs like Comprehensive Meta-Analysis, or David B. Wilson's online conversion tool: https://campbellcollaboration.org/escalc/html/EffectSizeCalculator-Home.php.

S13 EEF protocol 2019

Higgins, S. et al. (2019). EEF Evidence Database: Protocol and Analysis Plan, version 1.1, June 2019.

Location in the document: p. 11, 'Statistical procedures and conventions'

A random effects model will be adopted for each meta-analysis and the heterogeneity of the distribution of the effect sizes assessed using Q and I² (Higgins et al. 2009). A pre-specified set of coded study features will be further explored through moderator variable analysis under a mixed effects model, as potential sources of systematic variation.

The evidence summaries for each strand draw on a series of meta-analyses, completed in Autumn 2021 (EEF Evidence Database Phase 1), of the studies that were included in the reviews on which the previous version of the Toolkit was based (see Higgins et al. 2022 for a review of the methodologies). S15 EEF Phase 2 protocol 2024

Higgins, S. et al. (2024). EEF Evidence Database Phase 2: Protocol and Analysis Plan, January 2024.

Location in the document: 'Selection of studies'

Customised machine classifiers will be developed for each of the Toolkit strands to reduce the total number of studies that need to be screened manually. The aim is to create a search and screening process for each Toolkit strand which can then be used to update the strands as a series of linked 'living reviews' (Elliot et al. 2017). The studies will be screened using the 'priority screening' tools in EPPI-Reviewer 6 (Thomas et al. 2017).

S16 EEF protocol 2019

Higgins, S. et al. (2019). EEF Evidence Database: Protocol and Analysis Plan, version 1.1, June 2019.

Location in the document: pp. 7–9, 'Identifying the primary outcome from a study for the Toolkit database' and 'Statistical independence of findings from a single study'; Appendix G, p. 64, flow diagram 'Primary outcome effect size data extraction process' (S. Higgins, 16 Nov 2018, v05)

Identifying the best single outcome from a study is not always straightforward as the study aims are not necessarily the same as the Toolkit aims. The key principles adopted to support identification are: • A good test of the impact of the intervention for the Toolkit […] • An appropriate measure of educational attainment […] Standardised tests or national tests and examinations tend to be better overall indicators of educational performance than researcher-designed measures or teacher-designed class tests […] • As direct and fair a measure as possible. Simple outcomes rather than combined ones across subjects are usually preferable […] These considerations have resulted in a flow diagram to aid coders in identifying the primary outcome (see Appendix G) where the aim is to identify in each study the most comparable effect size for the Toolkit, but which also takes into account the nature of the particular intervention. […] We identify one primary outcome for the Toolkit strand from each study (see Appendix G). This is usually, but not necessarily the primary outcome of the study. Other equivalent academic and cognitive outcomes are recorded as secondary outcomes. Where it is not possible to identify a single preferred outcome […], comparable outcomes are combined to produce one overall effect for the study.

S17 EEF Phase 2 protocol 2024

Higgins, S. et al. (2024). EEF Evidence Database Phase 2: Protocol and Analysis Plan, January 2024.

Location in the document: pp. 7–8, 'Statistical procedures and conventions'

Where possible, a post-test comparison of the impact of the intervention or approach, adjusted for baseline and clustering of pupils in classes, will be selected as the primary outcome. If this is calculable from other reported data then this effect size will be used. Where this is not available the following order of preference will be used: • Post-test comparison adjusted for baseline (such as from ANCOVA or MLM/HLM); • Post-test only comparison (for randomised studies or matched studies where there is no or little baseline imbalance); • Gain score comparison (for non-randomised studies or where there is notable imbalance at baseline).

The 25 meta-analyses included by the pipeline but not used by the EEF

All 25 were found within the same publication window as the EEF’s own set: the identification queries were restricted to publication year ≤ 2018 — the year of the strand appendix we reproduce (its most recent meta-analysis is Zheng, 2016). The list is therefore a fuller harvest of the same period, not a forward extension; the post-2021 literature is handled separately in Step 7.

Each passed Stages 1–4 (title/abstract vote, full-text reading, consolidation, Opus verification) under the neutral prompt. Grouped by focus:

Self-regulated learning and learning-strategy instruction (10). Dignath & Büttner (2008); Donker-Bergstra et al. (2013); de Boer et al. (2018); Li et al. (2018); Jang & Shin (2011); Ko et al. (2016); Latipah (2010); Benz (2010); Lee et al. (2018); Guirguis & Pankowski (2017).

Writing, content-area and higher-order instruction (5). Graham et al. (2012); Bangert-Drowns et al. (2004); Swanson (2001); Scruggs et al. (2010); Maxwell & Grenier (2014).

Pupils with ADHD, emotional/behavioural or learning difficulties (6). Reid et al. (2005); Popham et al. (2018); Rapport et al. (2013); Cortese et al. (2015); Moore et al. (2018); Karch et al. (2013).

Early-childhood and universal self-regulation programmes (3). Baron et al. (2017); Pandey et al. (2018); Smithers et al. (2018).

General instruction (1). Marzano (1998).

Three are closely related to EEF sources rather than independent of them: Donker-Bergstra et al. (2013) is the report version of Donker et al. (2014), Dignath & Büttner (2008) shares its study base with Dignath et al. (2008), and de Boer et al. (2018) is the follow-up of de Boer et al. (2014). Several others sit at the edge of the construct (cognitive training for ADHD, the Tools of the Mind curriculum) and are natural candidates for the class-C adjudication proposed in Section 3.2. Together the 25 contributed 49 studies that the EEF database already holds — reached by the EEF through other routes — and several hundred it does not.
